stories.title: Fermat’s last theorem formalised by AI agents in just 11 days
stories.summary: Converting the proof of Fermat's last theorem into code that computers can check was expected to take years. Anthropic's Claude AI managed it in less than two weeks
stories.extract:
AI company Anthropic has created a formalised proof of Fermat’s last theorem. It took just 11 days for a group of AI agents to complete the task, confirming that the human-found proof proposed in the 1990s is correct.
Fermat’s last theorem puzzled mathematicians for centuries until it was proved in 1995 by Andrew Wiles. It states that there are no whole numbers a, b, and c that satisfy the equation aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ, where n is a whole number greater than 2.

stories.title: Neuroscientist debunks the idea that living in the past is bad. It’s great for mental health.
stories.extract:
People who love reminiscing about the good ol’ days are often criticized for living in the past and are told to keep looking forward. It makes sense. Often, people who become overly interested in the great times they had in high school are neglecting the fact that things can be just as good in the present. It almost feels like they peaked at a young age. It’s also dangerous to fall into the trap of seeing the past through rose-colored glasses and thinking that the world has gone downhill.

stories.title: Nations and big tech to train AI using ‘gold dust’ data from Ukraine
stories.summary: Foreign states and technology firms are scrambling for data from the Ukraine war so they can train the next-generation of AI models that might be used in defence and national security
stories.extract:
Global superpowers and giant technology firms are scrambling for real-world data from the war in Ukraine to build next-generation AI models that will empower militaries in future conflicts. Videos of drone strikes and other sensor data are like “gold dust” for training AI, say experts.

stories.title: Indian tea exhibition to be held in Windhoek
stories.extract:
The High Commission of India in Windhoek is hosting an exhibition on Indian tea at Grove Mall, which started on Tuesday and runs till 9 September.
The exhibition, the first Indian tea exhibition to be held in Namibia, will showcase the heritage, diversity and cultural significance of Indian tea, including varieties from Assam, Darjeeling and Nilgiri.
